title: Machine learning magnetic interactions from neutron powder diffraction data
authors: Adit S. Desai, Yongqiang Cheng, Joseph A. M. Paddison
abstract: Neutron diffraction is a versatile experimental technique capable of probing a material's magnetic properties. While diffraction is typically used to determine the magnetic structure of a material, magnetic diffuse scattering data from a diffraction experiment are also sensitive to the magnetic interactions in its Hamiltonian. However, accurately determining magnetic interaction parameters from neutron-scattering data involves an inverse scattering problem that is challenging to solve in general. Here, we investigate the effectiveness of a machine learning approach to predict the interaction parameters given magnetic diffuse-scattering data measured on powder samples, for a comprehensive survey of isotropic interactions on eight high-symmetry lattices. Across all lattices we considered, the machine-learning approach estimates the interaction parameters with high (~2%) accuracy, while avoiding the issue of false minima that is encountered with non-linear least squares refinement. Our results highlight that powder diffuse-scattering data can provide a compact "fingerprint" of the magnetic interactions for many materials.
summary: This work introduces a machine learning framework to solve the inverse problem of extracting magnetic interaction parameters from neutron diffuse scattering data. By training a neural network on simulated data across multiple lattices, the authors demonstrate high accuracy in parameter estimation. This provides a powerful, robust tool for characterizing magnetic interactions in condensed matter systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenging inverse scattering problem of accurately determining magnetic interaction parameters from diffuse neutron scattering data.
main_result: A machine learning approach successfully estimates interaction parameters with high accuracy, avoiding pitfalls like false minima encountered with traditional non-linear least-squares refinement.
method: The study trains a neural network on simulated diffuse scattering data generated across various high-symmetry lattices and interaction parameter sets.
model_or_system: The system involves magnetic materials modeled by the isotropic Heisenberg Hamiltonian, considering up to four nearest-neighbor interactions on eight high-symmetry lattices.
key_observables: Diffuse magnetic intensity S(Q), which serves as a 'fingerprint' of the magnetic interactions.
important_parameters: The reduced interaction parameter $\tilde{J}_n = J_n / T$, and the lattice structure (e.g., Honeycomb, BCC, Kagome).
main_assumptions: The approach is limited to high-symmetry lattices, and one assumption involves equating two types of symmetry-inequivalent third-neighbor interactions in certain lattices.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 8 lattices studied and show representative simulated diffuse S(Q) data for different interaction parameter sets, comparing ML performance against least-squares regression.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem, details the simulation setup (Hamiltonian, data generation), introduces the ML methodology (training, loss function), and validates the approach by comparing ML predictions against experimental data and traditional fitting techniques.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, the core methodology—using ML to solve an ill-posed inverse problem from complex experimental data—is highly relevant for analyzing quantum many-body systems where direct parameter extraction is difficult.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: The lattices studied in this paper and their four near neighbor magnetic interactions with pathways labeled J1, J2, J3 and J4. Note that the kagome and pyrochlore lattices have two types of symmetry-inequivalent third neighbors that can have different interactions; one of these is labeled J3 in the figure and the other is at double the vector corresponding to J1. In this work we assumed that both third-neighbor interactions are the same.
FIG. 2: Simulated magnetic diffuse S(Q) for the honeycomb lattice (top panel) and BCC lattice (bottom panel), with values of the interaction parameters labeled on the plots.

FIG. 3: Graphs demonstrating sensitivity of the simulated diffuse intensity S(Q) to differences in the magnetic interactions Jn. In each panel, the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) in S(Q) for a given lattice is plotted against the RMSD in the interaction values ˜Jn, for randomly-chosen pairs of simulations in the training data. Probability density is shown in false color.

FIG. 4: Schematic for training the neural network and applying it to experimental data. Blue blocks on the left show the process of training the neural network, and purple blocks on the right show the application to experimental data, which must first be fitted to a smoothing function and normalized before being input to the network.

FIG. 5: Learning curves of the neural network for validation data (red lines) and training data (blue lines). Each panel shows the loss defined in Eq. (7) as a function of the number of completed training loops (epochs) for the lattice indicated.
